items.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2bn fine for money laundering failings

items.title: What an economics Nobel Prize winner knows about pricing
items.author: Erika Ryan
items.summary: Nobel Prize winners Robert Hall and Michael Woodford are being honored for their research into economic stability and how forward-looking expectations influence business pricing decisions. Their work highlights the critical role of clear communication from policymakers in managing public expectations regarding inflation and economic cycles.

also.author: Eshe Nelson
also.title: Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford Awarded Nobel for Economics
also.note: The New York Times focuses on the formal announcement of the winners.

also.title: A Nobel prize for how to keep economies on an even keel
also.note: The Economist frames the story around the practical application of the winners' theories for maintaining economic equilibrium.

brief.what: Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics for their research on macroeconomic stability and the microeconomic factors that drive business pricing and consumer behavior.
brief.who: Robert Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University are the two American recipients of the award.
brief.context: The research focuses on how businesses set prices based not only on current costs but also on their expectations of future economic conditions. Woodford emphasizes that when businesses anticipate sustained cost increases, they adjust prices more rapidly than they would for temporary fluctuations.
brief.why: The Nobel committee recognized their work for providing insights into how to stabilize cycles of economic boom and bust. Woodford argues that policymakers must communicate clearly and predictably to ensure public expectations remain aligned with economic reality, as reactive policy alone is insufficient for long-term stability.

items.title: Preserve research data for tomorrow’s AI-enabled integrity checks
items.author: Qingde Shi
items.summary: Researchers are urged to preserve raw data to facilitate future integrity checks powered by artificial intelligence. This practice aims to ensure scientific transparency and verification as AI tools evolve.

brief.what: The editorial calls for the systematic preservation of research data to enable future AI-driven integrity verification. This approach is intended to support the ongoing validation of scientific findings as automated analysis tools become more sophisticated.
brief.who: Nature, the scientific journal, is the primary actor advocating for these data management standards.
brief.context: Scientific integrity relies on the ability to audit and verify research results, a process that is increasingly being augmented by machine learning and automated systems.
brief.why: The publication argues that preserving raw data is essential for tomorrow's AI-enabled integrity checks, ensuring that scientific records remain verifiable as technology advances.
